# area: overloads
# hypothesis: with overloads keyed on Literal[True] and Literal[False] plus a bool fallback, a bool-typed or union-typed argument must expand to both literal overloads, so the result is str | bytes; a checker that skips union expansion returns only the fallback type.
from typing import Literal, overload, reveal_type


@overload
def encode(data: str, binary: Literal[True]) -> bytes: ...
@overload
def encode(data: str, binary: Literal[False]) -> str: ...
@overload
def encode(data: str, binary: bool) -> str | bytes: ...
def encode(data: str, binary: bool) -> str | bytes:
    return data.encode() if binary else data


def use(flag: bool, lit: Literal[True, False]) -> None:
    reveal_type(encode("a", True))
    reveal_type(encode("a", False))
    reveal_type(encode("a", flag))
    reveal_type(encode("a", lit))


use(True, False)
print(encode("a", True), encode("a", False))
hypothesis: Overload resolution on a bool or Literal[True, False] argument expands to the Literal[True] and Literal[False] overloads, giving str | bytes, while a checker without union expansion returns only the bool fallback type.
